sequences.source_document: Schiffer et al. 2022, Tectonophysics 825, 229235 (PDF; XML abstract and captions)

steps.action: Pose the question of onshore crustal structure (Moho depth, crust-mantle transition, HVLC) around the Labrador Sea, Davis Strait and Baffin Bay, where only offshore constraints exist.
steps.quote: crustal models are limited onshore, which makes an interpretation of regional structures as well as the extent, and therefore origin of the DSIP

steps.action: State rival origins for HVLC (DSIP igneous, syn-rift serpentinised mantle, pre-existing metamorphosed lower crust or older serpentinised mantle) and announce a test of plate-tectonic versus plume-dominated formation of the Davis Strait.
steps.quote: determining whether it is generically related to the Davis Strait Igneous Province, syn-rift exhumed and serpentinised mantle, or pre-existing lower crustal bodies

steps.action: Compile published LAB, Moho, crystalline crust and sediment thickness models and extract HVLC presence and thickness from published refraction lines into maps of prior knowledge (Fig. 3).
steps.quote: which we have assembled into maps that illustrate the state of knowledge prior to our study

steps.action: Build a joint inversion of P-receiver functions and P-wave polarisation (apparent Vs) that combines linearised iterative least squares with a random model search, delay-time layer parameterisation and a Vs-dependent Vp/Vs lookup table.
steps.quote: with a new random model search scheme

steps.action: Run 1000 inversions per station from randomly drawn starting models (5 to 20 layers, Vs 1-5 km/s) so that the posterior population spreads over non-unique solutions; example convergence for 5, 12 and 18 layers shown in Fig. 4.
steps.quote: 1000 full linearised iterative LSQ inversion runs were calculated with a minimum of 15 iterations and vastly different starting models

steps.action: Collect broadband three-component teleseismic data from 24 stations (EIDA, IRIS, CNDC) and computed RFs from 10 temporary stations (GLImER), giving 3490 events.
steps.quote: This resulted in a total dataset of 3490 events for all stations

steps.action: Invert each station's data to a 10,000-model posterior population, weight the models by inverse data error, and take the weighted mean as the final model with a 95% interval as its uncertainty.
steps.quote: The applied inverse approach produces a distribution of 10,000 models for each station.

steps.action: Fix interpretation rules: crust-mantle transition bounds at Vs 4.25 and 4.4 km/s, top of HVLC at Vs about 4.1 km/s (visual, as low as 4.0), Moho gradient and HVLC treated as one unit, and 1 km subtracted from HVLC thickness for resolution.
steps.quote: we define the geological interfaces as follows

steps.action: Estimate station-wise Moho depths (about 32 to 47 km) with uncertainties and crust-mantle transition thicknesses (Table 1, Fig. 6).
steps.quote: show values that range between ~32 km and ~ 47 km

steps.action: Check the Moho estimates against independent regional crustal models and against earlier RF estimates at the same stations (Darbyshire 2003, Dahl-Jensen et al. 2003, 2016, Kumar et al. 2007, Postlethwaite et al. 2014, Vervaet & Darbyshire 2022).
steps.quote: which is therefore a good first indication that the estimates are geologically meaningful

steps.action: Estimate HVLC thickness at each station: 4-5 km in the Disko Bay area and on the Cumberland Peninsula, 1-3 km elsewhere, negligible at TULEG, ILUG/ILULI and NRS (Fig. 8).
steps.quote: there are clear indications of HVLC in the Disko Bay area with thicknesses of 4–5 km

steps.action: Compare Moho estimates with the reference model (RMS 3.7 km West Greenland, 5.5 km Canada; 25 of 34 deeper) and relate Moho variations to tectonic provinces along margin transects (Fig. 7, Fig. 9).
steps.quote: there is a systematic tendency of the RF inversion (and interpretation of the velocity models) towards a deeper Moho

steps.action: Derive the spatial signatures expected of each HVLC type: igneous near DSIP volcanics and in thinned crust, orogenic near sutures and in thickened crust, serpentinised mantle where HVLC contacts sediments.
steps.quote: lower crustal intrusions may more commonly appear in regions of thinned crust, whilst orogenic-type HVLC rather occurs in thickened crust

steps.action: Assign station HVLC to types by spatial correlation with mapped volcanics, terrane boundaries and crustal thickness, region by region (Figs. 8 and 10).
steps.quote: the estimated HVLC in the Disko Bay area corresponds well with mapped occurrences of igneous rocks in the region

steps.action: Reject a DSIP igneous origin for HVLC at NANL (no nearby Mesozoic-Cenozoic magmatism) and in the Ketilidian and Makkovik provinces, preferring orogenic HVLC there.
steps.quote: An igneous interpretation of this HVLC relating to the DSIP is unlikely

steps.action: Place the interpreted HVLC bodies on a 62 Ma plate reconstruction to test whether bodies of the same type line up across the conjugate margins (Fig. 11).
steps.quote: The relative location of HVLC bodies at 62 Ma using a reconstruction

steps.action: Revise the Cumberland Peninsula HVLC from an igneous candidate to a more likely orogenic origin because it is misaligned with the igneous belt and lines up with the conjugate suture in the reconstruction.
steps.quote: Instead, HVLC on the Cumberland Peninsula may be more likely of orogenic origin

steps.action: Keep the regional interpretation: the DSIP extends further north in West Greenland, part of the Davis Strait HVLC is inherited orogenic crust, and inheritance plays a major role; the plume question is left undetermined.
steps.quote: We suggest that the DSIP continues further north on the West Greenland margin than previously mapped.

end.claim: The DSIP likely extends further north in West Greenland than mapped, substantial HVLC beneath Davis Strait and near sutures is inherited orogenic crust, and structural inheritance plays a major role in localising breakup and magmatism.

decisive_move.sentence: Without the station-wise joint RF and P-polarisation inversion yielding onshore HVLC thicknesses and Moho depths, there would be no onshore HVLC distribution to interpret.

gates.evidence: Data were all available stations, not chosen by a hypothesis ('we have collected all available teleseismic data', §0 ¶1). Moho estimates faced comparison with independent models and earlier RF studies, which could have failed (p. 11, p. 14); HVLC origins rest on spatial correlation and a plate reconstruction with no decisive test, and the announced plate-versus-plume test ends with 'cannot be determined' (p. 20). The interface thresholds are stated, but the HVLC top was picked by 'a visual interpretation of the model' (p. 11), and nothing is reported as fixed before the data.

Water-level deconvolution with Gaussian low-pass filtering

limits: The supplied XML text holds only the abstract and figure/table captions, so body steps are cited to printed pages and quoted from the PDF text. No review file, and no supplement despite the online supplementary data, was supplied; the acknowledgements mention three anonymous reviewers, so a review sequence cannot be coded. Sub-claims at other statuses: Moho depths per station are estimate_with_resolution (p. 11, Table 1); Moho variation by tectonic province is a regularity_in_range across 34 stations (inference, p. 16, p. 20); the plate-versus-plume hypothesis announced on p. 3 ends without a conclusion ('cannot be determined', p. 20); the HVLC along the Labrador Sea margins has no preferred model (p. 19); the HVLC at NUUK, PAAG and IVIG is left uncertain (pp. 18-19). The 1D assumption and lateral smearing may mimic Moho gradients and HVLC (p. 11). The HVLC top is partly picked visually. The paper does not report testing the sensitivity of the results to the Vp/Vs lookup table, the water level, or the 1 km subtraction (inference from absence).

disagreements.target: Regional crustal reference models ( [...] and Hall 2013; Welford et al. 2018; Lebedeva-Ivanova et al. 2019; CRUST1.0)
disagreements.support: RF Moho is systematically deeper (25 of 34 stations; RMS differences 3.7 and 5.5 km), and the north-south Moho trend on Baffin Island is reversed.
disagreements.quote: Curiously, this is the opposite trend than what the reference crustal model depicts.

disagreements.target: Kumar et al. (2007) RF Moho estimates at UPNV and GDH
disagreements.support: This paper and two other RF studies find Moho about 36-38 km where Kumar et al. found 32 km.
disagreements.quote: Only Kumar et al. (2007) estimated a substantially shallower Moho depth of 32 km at station UPNV.

disagreements.target: Postlethwaite et al. (2014) Moho estimates on the Labrador coast
disagreements.support: NANL is over 10 km deeper and MKVL (45 km) far deeper than their 26 km; Vervaet & Darbyshire (2022) support the deeper value.
disagreements.quote: but again considerably thicker than the estimate of 26 km by Postlethwaite et al. (2014).

disagreements.target: Darbyshire (2003) and Postlethwaite et al. (2014) at GFNU
disagreements.support: RF inversion gives a 40-45 km Moho transition, about 5-7.5 km deeper than these estimates.
disagreements.quote: but ~5–7.5 km deeper than estimates by Darbyshire (2003) and ~ 5 km deeper than estimates by Postlethwaite et al. (2014)

disagreements.target: Louden and Fan (1998) controlled-source models of the Makkovik Province
disagreements.support: MKVL Moho is about 13 km deeper, consistent with an independent RF code; the authors suggest a complex crust-mantle transition.
disagreements.quote: this estimate is ~13 km deeper than the reference model and published controlled source seismic models in the Makkovik Province

disagreements.target: Igneous interpretation of Davis Strait HVLC (Funck et al. 2007; Gerlings et al. 2009; Funck et al. 2012; Keen et [...]
disagreements.support: Correlation with sutures and analogy with lower-crustal flow models for the Greenland-Iceland-Faroes Ridge suggest part of the HVLC is deformed metamorphosed crust.
disagreements.quote: rather than entirely from igneous processes, as often assumed

disagreements.target: Serpentinised-mantle interpretation of Labrador Sea margin HVLC (Chian and Louden 1994; Chian et al. 1995b; Chalmers 1997)
disagreements.support: HVLC beneath intact continental crust is unlikely to be hydrated, so an igneous origin is possible.
disagreements.quote: [...] that all HVLC along the Labrador Sea conjugate margins could potentially be of igneous nature

disagreements.target: Previous RF studies based on H-κ stacking
disagreements.support: Single-layer crust cannot resolve crust-mantle transition zones or HVLC; this paper treats all stations with one inversion method.
disagreements.quote: Most previous RF estimates were based on H-κ stacking, which treats the crust as a single layer

disagreements.target: Previously mapped extent of the DSIP
disagreements.support: HVLC at northern West Greenland stations near volcanics suggests the province extends further north.
disagreements.quote: We suggest that the DSIP continues further north on the West Greenland margin than previously mapped.
